newsitem.title: RUSSIA: People want roubles, Russia mulls whether to sell.
newsitem.headline: People want roubles, Russia mulls whether to sell.

text.p: Everyone wants roubles but hints of inflation have put the Central Bank of Russia between a rock and a hard place and led it to indirectly raise Treasury bill yields, economists said on Tuesday.

Essentially a victim of its own success, Russia is seeing billions of dollars in portfolio investment, international loans and repatriated funds pour into the country, creating a demand for the modest rouble.

The dilemma facing the central bank is whether to risk inflation by letting roubles into the economy, which badly needs cash to start growing, or to soak up the new roubles, known as sterilising them, risking rouble appreciation.

If the rouble appreciates in real terms, Russian companies face tougher export terms. An overstrong rouble could be abandoned by investors, forcing a currency crisis as the Czech Republic has just faced.
The bank has been sterilising the inflows for several months by selling Treasury bills, prices of which have fallen for the first time in months.

Central bank first deputy chairman Sergei Aleksashenko said seasonal factors would stimulate year end inflation and predicted December inflation of about one percent and January 0.3-0.4 percent. It was 0.9 percent in July.
Economists say bankers should be happy to face their current dilemma since they confront it from a position of strength based on increased confidence in Russia, economists say.

"The central bank is extremely strong, probably stronger than at any time since reforms began," said Pavel Teplukhin, chief economist at Russian investment bank Troika Dialog. "And that strength is based on high international reserves."
Net international reserves, effectively growing on proceeds of T-bill sales, almost doubled in July to 60.9 trillion roubles ($10.5 billion) from 31.3 trillion in June, the bank said.
But more T-bills on offer have pushed down prices. Even so M2 money supply grew seven percent in June, while inflation in July edged up for the first time since June 1995.
Year on year inflation in July was 14.7 percent after 14.5 percent in June.
Teplukhin predicted the rouble would be allowed to appreciate about one percent in real terms through the end of the year on 5.5 percent second half inflation and 4.5 percent depreciation.

He said that low production costs, about 20-25 percent for natural resources which are the bulk of Russian exports, meant the real effect on exporters would be a relatively low one quarter of a percent price appreciation.

He said the central bank might begin issuing new bonds, essentially reverse repos which would allow it to temporarily soak up inflationary roubles. "For stability the central bank should pay a cost, and the cost is the interest on the loans."

Moscow investment bank Renaissance Capital economist Roland Nash said short term the central bank was likely to tighten monetary policy by selling more T-bills from its portfolio, continuing the August reversal of a trend to falling rates.
Yields on a paper maturing in May of next year rose 1.24 percent in the first half of the month.
"There is room for further monetary tightening," Nash said. "This could results in either a continuation of current flat yields or even a slight backup."
Khalid Sheikh, senior economist for Central and Eastern Europe at Dutch bank ABN Amro said the central bank needed to risk slight inflation to give the economy the roubles it needed to begin growing.
"They have reached a certain level of inflation that is line with economic development," he said. "Monetary policy has been very tight. Now they need to sustain economic growth."
